identity_evidence.quote: A 79-year-old Caucasian female presented to the emergency department

attribution_limitations: Day counting for the first sodium drop differs: the case text places the drop to 126 meq/l on the fourth day following admission (the sentence itself carries no day), the discussion says hyponatremia was first found on the third day, and Table 3 prints an onset of 3 days (126 meq/l) post-amiodarone.

SOURCE CONFLICT on the day of the sodium nadir (110 meq/l): the discussion says the sixth day, whereas the case text gives 124 meq/l on the sixth day and 113 meq/l on the seventh day with the nadir reached in less than 24 hours after that, and Table 3 prints 7 days (110 meq/l). The nadir value itself is not in conflict.

The later sodium values are said to occur "on day 13 and 135 meq/l on day 18 after discharge", but the discussion calls 135 meq/l normalization nine days after discontinuation on the ninth day (consistent with hospital day 18) and Table 3 prints Day 18 (135 meq/l); the phrase "after discharge" is inconsistent with that day count and no discharge date or discharge event is stated.

Table 3 current-case row trend cells ("Day 7 (112 meq/l)", "Day 18 (135 meq/l)") sit under the column "Day of First Na Increase and Trend" whose day base is not defined; Table 2 and the text give 113 meq/l on the seventh day. The value 112 is kept as a review_only observation and not treated as a conflict or merged.

Unit and print inconsistencies: serum osmolality prints as Osm/l in Table 2 but Osm/kg in the text; Table 2 prints random urine creatinine as mg/ml and random urine sodium as meq/ml; the Table 1 and Table 2 glomerular filtration rate reference range prints mg/dl for a ml/min quantity; the Figure 1 y-axis prints meq/dl for sodium whereas the text uses meq/l. Values and units are kept exactly as printed.

The text sentences giving serum and urine osmolarity and the fractional excretions of sodium and urate carry the same numbers as Table 2 rows (seventh day) but name no day and are not tied to the table, so they are kept as separate review_only observations and not merged with the table facts.

Causal wording about amiodarone is mixed: the case text says amiodarone was suspected to have been the offending agent, the discussion says careful evaluation made it clear that the hyponatremia was induced by amiodarone, and also that whether withdrawal alone would have resolved it is unclear. The recurrence on day 10 is hedged as "likely due to" desmopressin and dextrose 5% water.

Cumulative amiodarone amounts in the discussion (3,200 mg when hyponatremia was first found on the third day; an additional 600 mg for 3,800 mg before the nadir) are not derivable from the dosing in the case text (400 mg three times per day from the first day of admission, then reduced to 400 mg daily and 200 mg daily).

Table 3 lists published cases other than the present patient (rows citing other first authors); only the row labelled "current case" is this patient. The Table 3 baseline sodium (134 meq/l) equals the Table 1 admission sodium and the pre-drop value in the text, but the source does not say they are the same measurement; the discussion also says sodium had been stable for months without values.

Several day-4 and day-6 findings (repeated chest X-ray, brain natriuretic peptide, sodium 126 meq/l, the physical examination, CT of the head, repeat sodium 124 meq/l, the hydrochlorothiazide stop) follow a sentence that carries the day but their own sentences state no day; they are not given the time of a neighbouring sentence.

Pulmonary edema is stated only as "the clinical picture of pulmonary edema" and congestive heart failure only as a confounding etiology, without a diagnostic basis; both are kept at provisional or unknown verification.
